Two weeks later the tablets were still in their boxes. The training date had slipped twice. The first batch of data arrived on paper. Each time Chinmay asked, Eshaan said, "Almost there," and smiled. Eshaan let out a long breath. "Half the villages have no charging points."

You want to know my biggest early mistake as a manager? Siddharth. He'd sit in every sprint planning, nod, and say, "Yep, doable." Then the week would end and his tasks would be untouched. Not late by a day. Untouched. I thought he was lazy, honestly. I nearly wrote him up.
Then a colleague said, "Manoj, have you ever seen anyone say no in your meetings?" I thought about it. Nobody had. I'd built a room where "yes" was the only safe word.
So I started ending planning with, "Okay, what here do you think is a bad idea?" and then waiting, awkwardly long. The third time, Siddharth said, "The API migration. It's going to break the billing system." He was right. We rescheduled it. His tasks started getting done.

qa.q: What did Siddharth say about the API migration?
qa.a: "It's going to break the billing system."

qa.q: Why might Siddharth have said 'Yep, doable' while leaving tasks untouched?
qa.a: In a room where only yes felt safe, he likely couldn't voice his disagreement, so it came out as quiet non-delivery.

qa.q: What change did Manoj make, and why did it work?
qa.a: Ending planning by asking what was a bad idea and then waiting, which made 'no' safe and let Siddharth raise the real risk. 🤔

qa.q: How might the colleague have seen Manoj's meetings?
qa.a: As a place where everyone nodded along, which is why the colleague asked whether anyone had ever said no.

grounding: A manager recalls a team member who agreed in every meeting and then delivered nothing, and how making it safe to say no changed things.

I'm Kalyani, and I head the science department at a school in Kolkata. In June I proposed moving Class 9 practicals to a new project-based format. Everyone agreed, Arnab included. "Sounds good," he said, nodding.
By August his section hadn't started. The planning sheet was blank. The rubric he'd promised by the 15th never came. Each time I asked, he smiled: "Almost there."
I don't know what was going on in his head. But it slowly struck me that I had never heard him say what he actually thought of the plan. In that June meeting, three senior teachers had spoken warmly for it first. Maybe "sounds good" was the only answer that felt available.
So I stopped chasing the rubric. Over tea I said, "Arnab, I may have rushed that meeting. If you think this format is wrong for your section, I really want to hear it. You won't be in trouble."
He put down his cup. "Honestly? I think it'll eat all the revision time."

qa.q: What did Arnab say each time Kalyani asked about the rubric?
qa.a: "Almost there."

qa.q: How did Kalyani feel as she thought back on Arnab's "sounds good"?
qa.a: Kalyani felt uneasy and a little regretful, suspecting she had rushed the meeting and that Arnab couldn't disagree after three senior teachers praised the plan.

qa.q: Which choice by Kalyani opened the real conversation?
qa.a: Dropping the chasing, admitting the meeting may have been rushed, and saying Arnab could disagree without trouble, which let him name his worry about revision time.

qa.q: What might the June meeting have felt like for Arnab?
qa.a: With senior teachers already praising the plan, Arnab may have felt that disagreeing would look difficult or disloyal, so agreeing seemed safer.

At twenty-six, I was a new manager at a printing press in Indore. One man, Prakash, older than me, always nodded in meetings. "Yes, sir, good plan." Then every milestone slipped. The binding was late. The proofs were late. I thought he was lazy. Then one day, I found his notebook on the table. On the page from our first meeting, he'd written: "This will not work. Paper is wrong." He'd never said it. So I did something I hadn't done before. I called him in, closed the door and said, "Prakash, if you think a plan won't work, I want to hear it. You won't get in trouble for saying no." He was quiet for a long time. Then he told me everything wrong with the plan. He was right.

I'm Bhupen, and in my first year as a team lead at the bank's back office, I had a problem called Ishita. In every meeting she nodded. "Yes, we can finish the audit prep by the fifteenth." "Yes, I'll take the vendor files." And then nothing arrived on time. Not late enough to be dramatic, just always a little late.

Supervisor's note, community health project, 30 July.

At the June planning meeting Anand agreed to finish the village survey by the tenth of July. He said, "No problem." The tenth passed, then the twentieth. Each week his update is cheerful and vague: "Almost there." He is not lazy; his field notes are excellent.

Looking back, I think I pushed the plan through fast. Anand was the newest person in the room and the only one who knows the hill villages, where roads close in the rains. He never said so.

Today I met him alone, not to scold. I said, "I may have given you a deadline you couldn't argue with. If the plan doesn't work, I want to hear it from you, not from the calendar." He was quiet, then said, "The monsoon cuts off two villages till August." We have reset the date to the end of August.

Binita

Third missed milestone. Alka said yes to the new reporting format in the April meeting. She even nodded when I asked, "Everyone comfortable?" Since then: the first draft came two days late, the second never came, and today's check-in she said, "Working on it," and looked away. She is not lazy. She stays late, she helps juniors. Tomorrow I'll ask her for a coffee, just us, and say clearly, "You can tell me this plan doesn't work. I'd rather know." I need to mean it, even if it means redoing my slides.
Sabina
